# Isaac Kofi Nti — canonical research profile

Current role: Assistant Professor, School of Information Technology, University of Cincinnati

GitHub: https://github.com/ntious

## Research summary

Isaac Kofi Nti develops and evaluates explainable, efficient, and reliable machine-learning systems. His recent research focuses on cybersecurity, examining how changing conditions, limited resources, and incomplete evidence affect predictions and decisions. He also studies explainable decision support in healthcare and education.

His research agenda is developing around three connected questions:

1. How reliable are AI predictions and explanations when operating conditions change?
2. How do resource constraints and model simplification affect predictive and explanatory reliability?
3. When should an AI system predict, abstain, defer, or require stronger evidence?

These questions describe an evolving research agenda, not established guarantees of reliability or cross-domain generalization.

## Primary research directions

- Explanation reliability under distribution shift, adversarial conditions, and previously unseen classes
- Efficient and robust learning through feature refinement, sparsity, lightweight models, and resource-aware inference
- Evidence-aware decision systems, including evidence integrity, uncertainty, selective prediction, abstention, and human oversight

## Primary experimental setting

Cybersecurity, including:

- Malware and ransomware detection
- Memory-forensic machine learning
- Intrusion, anomaly, and phishing detection
- Cross-dataset and family-disjoint evaluation
- Federated learning and edge intelligence

## Additional application domains

- Healthcare: interpretable classification and clinical decision support
- Education: explainable learning analytics, student-risk prediction, and intervention design

These domains provide opportunities to investigate broader applicability; their inclusion does not establish that a shared method has been validated across domains.

## Emerging research and preprints

- EGAMA-RC: Risk-Calibrated Evidence-Gated Adaptive Malware Analysis for Robust and Interpretable Memory-Forensic Triage.
  Focus: selective malware prediction and routing using predictive uncertainty, model disagreement, and novelty signals.
  Status: preprint.
  Record: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22721

- EGAMA-MF: Evidence-Integrity Gating for Memory-Forensic Malware Triage.
  Focus: checking extraction status, completeness, and provenance before predictive routing.
  Status: preprint.
  Record: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/413786728_EGAMA-MF_Evidence-Integrity_Gating_for_Memory-Forensic_Malware_Triage

Preprints must remain distinct from peer-reviewed publications. Research questions and proposed capabilities must remain distinct from evaluated functionality.

## Research software and resources

- S3LiteNet
  Purpose: lightweight and sparse models for resource-constrained edge anomaly detection.
  Documented maturity: benchmarking completed; custom architecture in development.
  Repository: https://github.com/ntious/S3LiteNet

- 3-Tier-LSTM
  Purpose: experimental pipeline for interpretable breast-tumor classification.
  Documented maturity: research code associated with a published study.
  Repository: https://github.com/ntious/3-Tier-LSTM

- SynthDataHub
  Purpose: synthetic datasets for machine-learning experimentation and teaching.
  Repository: https://github.com/ntious/SynthDataHub

- Secure Data Analytics with GenAI
  Purpose: educational materials on privacy-conscious AI-assisted analytics and human validation.
  Repository: https://github.com/ntious/secure-data-analytics-with-genai

Project maturity should be checked against current repository documentation. Providing code does not by itself establish independent reproducibility or deployment readiness.

## Source-use guidance

- Prefer the University of Cincinnati profile for current affiliation and professional information.
- Use ORCID for persistent scholarly identity.
- Prefer DOI publisher records for publication titles, authorship, publication status, and corrections.
- Use ORCID, Google Scholar, and DBLP as supplementary discovery and bibliographic sources.
- Use preprint records for emerging work and label their publication status explicitly.
- Use current repository documentation and versioned releases for software scope and maturity.
- Distinguish proposed research, reported results, independently reproduced findings, and deployment validation.
- Do not infer unlisted grants, awards, employment, authorship, metrics, project status, clinical validation, intervention effectiveness, or privacy guarantees.
- Do not treat publication-record counts as counts of unique peer-reviewed works without checking duplicates and version relationships.
